title: The Book That Reads You Back

blocks.c: The Book That Reads You Back

Most apps introduce themselves with a slideshow. Arrows, dots, a button marked Skip that everyone presses. We would rather not spend your first minute that way. This is a book, and you are already reading it — which means the tour has already begun, and you are, if we may say so, doing rather well.

Here is the arrangement. Each chapter of this book teaches one part of the app, in the place where that part actually lives. Nothing is required of you. You can read straight through and touch nothing, and the app will go on quietly working the way it works. But when a chapter invites you to try something, the thing it names will be on the screen in front of you, close enough to reach. That is the design principle of this whole application: around here, the book is the interface.

Begin with the pages themselves. That quiet bar at the bottom of this page — the one that looks like a design flourish — is how you turn pages. Tap the right side and the book obliges. Tap the left and it takes you back, no questions asked. Or ignore it entirely and swipe, the way you would nudge a real page you were not quite done with.

If your copy of this book is scrolling instead of turning, that is a mode, not a mistake. Some readers scroll; the app respects that, and the whole of chapter two is about choosing. For now, whichever way the text moves is the right way.

Next, touch the middle of the page once, on the prose itself. The header and its buttons step out of the room; the words stay. Touch again and the furniture comes back. A book should be mostly book. The controls here know they are staff, not family, and they wait to be called.

While the header is visible, look at its left corner. The chevron steps back the way you came, one screen at a time. Beside it sits a small diamond — the app's own mark — and that one goes all the way home, to your shelf, from anywhere in the app. You cannot get lost here. There is always a door, and it is always in the same place.
A reader's attention is a loan, not a gift. An interface repays it by getting out of the way.

One more thing before chapter two, and it requires nothing of you at all. Your place in this book is already saved. It was saved when you opened it, it has been saved as you read, and it will be saved if you leave in the middle of a sentence, which you are welcome to do. There is no bookmark to remember, because the app does the remembering. That is its job, not yours.
This is the owner's tour of the Offline Reader, written as a book because a reading app is best explained where the reading happens. It ships inside the app and never touches the network.
